P10d: Most institutions end up with more and more layers and offices as they get older. The Zapatistas took stock of theirs, and they moved authority down. They didn't write a leadership book and open up a certification program, they changed the system they were actually living in.

P12d: One thing the Zapatistas have been clear about is that people shouldn't import or export Zapatismo as a ready-made model. The useful thing isn't their diagram, though. It's how they learn: they build things and ask questions, and when they find out where the practice isn't working, they change the structure.
P12g: One thing the Zapatistas have been clear about is that people shouldn't import or export Zapatismo as a ready-made model. The useful thing to copy is how they learn, though. They build things and ask questions, and when they find out where the practice isn't working, they change the structure.
P13d: They also don't prove my whole economic path, the one where unpriced internal necessities come first, then a common purse, and then you get rid of outside money. Zapatista communities do use collective work to support their schools and clinics. They support their autonomous government and their resistance that way too. But they also sell products and trade, and they get support from outside. What they do show is that major necessities and public functions can be taken out of ordinary market purchase and governed collectively. Outside help can build capability. It can also create gatekeepers, and uneven dependence, when the specialist or the donor or the organization stays indispensable.

P14x: As part of celebrating the 10th anniversary of their autonomous governments, the Zapatistas opened up the Escuelita. Outsiders would live with families and learn autonomy by participating in the day to day life there. The first sessions had about 1,500 students, and later sessions had thousands more.

P15f: One way an escuelita could fail is if it becomes a business, where residents' lives turn into a performance of community for paying outsiders, and success gets measured by how many people come instead of how many daughter communities get started. A week of feeling transformed isn't what it's for. It's for teaching enough of the social and material system that some people can build it somewhere else.
